tt_kinh_duoc_su.tom_tat: The Sūtra of the Merit and Virtue of the Past Vows of Medicine Master Vaidūrya Light Tathāgata, translated from Xuanzang's Chinese by BTTS, expounding the 12 Great Vows, the Eastern Pure Land, healing dharani, and protection of the 12 Yaksha Generals.
tt_kinh_duoc_su.noi_dung:
SŪTRA OF THE MERIT AND VIRTUE OF THE PAST VOWS OF MEDICINE MASTER VAIDŪRYAPRABHĀ TATHĀGATA

(The Medicine Buddha Sūtra — Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaidūryaprabharāja Sūtra)

Translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty
English Translation referencing the Buddhist Text Translation Society (BTTS / City of Ten Thousand Buddhas) and BDK English Tripiṭaka Series

INCENSE PRAISE

The incense in the censer is now ignited,
Its fragrant smoke diffuses throughout the Dharma Realm.
The ocean-wide assembly of Buddhas perceive it from afar,
Gathering auspicious clouds in every place.
Sincere hearts manifesting in all directions,
The Buddhas reveal their golden bodies.
Namo Incense Cloud Canopy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (3 times)

PRAISE OF THE WILLOW BRANCH

From the willow branch, sweet dew is sprinkled across the three-thousand worlds,
Purifying the defilements of nature, speech, and mind.
Devas and humans rejoice, diseases and sorrows vanish,
Flames of suffering transform into pure golden lotuses.
Namo Bodhisattva of the Clear and Cool Realm Mahāsattva. (3 times)

HOMAGE TO THE BUDDHAS

With utmost sincerity, we prostrate to the Ever-Abiding Triple Gem of the Ten Directions. (1 bow)
With utmost sincerity, we prostrate to Fundamental Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha. (1 bow)
With utmost sincerity, we prostrate to Eastern Land Vaidūryanirbhāsa Master of Healing, Lapis Lazuli Light Tathāgata. (3 bows)
With utmost sincerity, we prostrate to Sūryaprabha Bodhisattva and Candraprabha Bodhisattva. (1 bow)
With utmost sincerity, we prostrate to the Assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Medicine Master Sūtra. (1 bow)

OPENING GĀTHĀ

The supreme, profound, and wondrous Dharma,
In hundreds of thousands of myriad kalpas is rarely encountered.
I now have seen and heard, and am able to receive and uphold it,
May I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.

THE SŪTRA TEXT

Thus have I heard. Once the Bhagavān was traveling through various countries to teach living beings. He arrived at Vaiśālī and stayed beneath the tree from which music resounded, together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus and thirty-six thousand Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, as well as kings, great ministers, brahmans, lay disciples, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and nonhumans. This boundless great multitude reverently surrounded the Buddha, and the World-Honored One expounded the Dharma for them.

At that time, the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, receiving the spiritual power of the Buddha, arose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, and joined his palms toward the Bhagavān, saying: "World-Honored One! We pray that You will speak about the names, past great vows, and supreme virtues of the Buddhas, so that living beings who hear them may eradicate karmic hindrances and bring benefit, peace, and joy to all beings in the Dharma-Ending Age."

The Buddha praised Mañjuśrī, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! With boundless compassion, you request that I speak on the names and vows of the Buddhas in order to sever the karmic bonds of living beings and bestow peace upon them. Listen attentively and consider this well; I shall now proclaim it to you."

Mañjuśrī replied: "Please speak, World-Honored One. We listen with joyous hearts."

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Eastward from here, past Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of ten Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Pure Vaidūrya (Vaidūryanirbhāsa). The Buddha of that land is named Medicine Master Vaidūrya Light Tathāgata (Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaidūryaprabharāja), Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, Perfected in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed Lord, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Devas and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. When that World-Honored One was practicing the Bodhisattva Way in the past, he brought forth Twelve Great Vows to cause all sentient beings to obtain whatever they seek."

THE TWELVE GREAT VOWS

The First Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Unexcelled Complete Enlightenment, a brilliant radiance will blaze forth from my body, illuminating limitless, boundless, and infinite worlds. My body will be adorned with the thirty-two major marks of excellence and the eighty minor characteristics. I shall cause all living beings to become equal to me, with bodies possessing identical grandeur and radiance.'

The Second Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, my body will be like lapis lazuli, translucent inside and out, completely spotless, possessing magnificent splendor and vast virtue. My body will dwell securely within a web of dazzling light exceeding the radiance of the sun and moon, illuminating all beings wandering in darkness, so that they may awaken and act according to their aspirations in all good ways.'

The Third Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, through boundless wisdom and skillful means, I shall grant all sentient beings inexhaustible necessities for life, so that no one shall ever suffer from lack or deprivation.'

The Fourth Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if living beings walk upon heterodox paths, I shall lead them securely onto the path of Bodhi; and if they follow the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles, I shall establish them firmly in the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna).'

The Fifth Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if limitless living beings cultivate pure conduct within my Dharma, I shall enable them to observe the precepts perfectly with all three groups of pure precepts intact. Even if they have transgressed the precepts, upon hearing my name, they shall regain purity and never fall into the evil destinies.'

The Sixth Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if living beings suffer from bodily infirmities—being deformed, blind, deaf, mute, lame, hunchbacked, leprous, insane, or afflicted with various diseases—upon hearing my name, all shall be healed, endowed with sound faculties and handsome form.'

The Seventh Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if living beings are oppressed by severe illness, destitute, without shelter, physician, or medicine, without relatives and in desperate distress, once my name passes through their ears, their illnesses will be thoroughly cured, and they will experience supreme physical and mental peace, abundant family relations, and rapid spiritual progress.'

The Eighth Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if women who are deeply tormented by the hundreds of tribulations of womanhood wish to be free from female form, upon hearing my name, all will transform into men endowed with noble marks in subsequent rebirths, advancing toward supreme enlightenment.'

The Ninth Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, I shall liberate all sentient beings from the snares of Māra and release them from the shackles of perverse views. I shall gather them into right views, gradually teaching and guiding them to cultivate Bodhisattva practices and swiftly awaken to supreme enlightenment.'

The Tenth Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if living beings are imprisoned, chained, condemned to punishment, or face execution, suffering grief and misery from royal authority, upon hearing my name, through the awesome spiritual virtue of my blessings, they will be freed from all sorrow and tribulations.'

The Eleventh Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if living beings tormented by hunger and thirst commit evil deeds in search of food, upon hearing my name and mindfully reciting it, I shall first satisfy them with exquisite food and drink, and subsequently nourish them with the supreme flavor of the Dharma in lasting peace.'

The Twelfth Great Vow: 'I vow that in a future life, when I attain Bodhi, if living beings are destitute, lacking clothing, tormented day and night by cold, heat, mosquitoes, and flies, upon hearing my name and holding it in mind, they will obtain magnificent clothing suited to their wishes, along with precious ornaments, music, fragrances, and floral garlands in abundant fulfillment.'

THE SPLENDOR OF VAIDŪRYANIRBHĀSA AND DELIVERANCE

The Buddha continued: "Mañjuśrī, these are the Twelve Sublime Vows made by Medicine Master Vaidūrya Light Tathāgata when he walked the Bodhisattva Way. The splendor and virtues of that Buddha-land are equal to those of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī). The ground is made of pure lapis lazuli; the city walls, gates, pavilions, and balconies are constructed of the seven precious jewels. In that land, there are no evil paths, no suffering, and no women. Two foremost Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas assist that Buddha: Sūryaprabha (Sunlight) and Candraprabha (Moonlight). They lead the great assembly and uphold the treasury of true Dharma."

"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if sentient beings fall into greed, stinginess, and malice, hoarding wealth and refusing to give even a tiny portion to the needy, upon their death they will descend into the realm of hungry ghosts or animals. Yet if in their former human existence they ever heard the name of Medicine Master Vaidūrya Light Tathāgata, even for an instant, that name will suddenly arise in their memory in the lower realms. Immediately freed from suffering, they will be reborn among humans, mindful of karmic consequences, joyful in generosity, and practicing the six perfections."

"If living beings take the eight precepts or Mahāyāna vows and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Amitābha Buddha, yet their faith is not completely firm, if they hear the name of Medicine Master Vaidūrya Light Tathāgata, eight great Bodhisattvas—Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, Akṣayamati, Ratnacandana, Bhaiṣajyarāja, Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, and Maitreya—will descend from the heavens to guide them directly to rebirth in the Pure Land amidst jeweled lotus flowers."

THE MEDICINE MASTER DHĀRAṆĪ

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the samādhi named *Dispelling the Sufferings of All Sentient Beings*. Having entered this concentration, a brilliant ray shone forth from his uṣṇīṣa, and he proclaimed the Great Dhāraṇī:

namo bhagavate bhaiṣajyaguru-vaidūryaprabharājāya tathāgatāya arhate samyaksambuddhāya tadyathā:
oṃ bhaiṣajye bhaiṣajye bhaiṣajya-samudgate svāhā.

"When the Buddha had spoken this mantra from within the light, the great earth trembled and emanated boundless light. All diseases were cured, and all beings experienced serenity and joy. If any man or woman is afflicted with severe illness, they should wash and purify themselves, rinse their mouth, and recite this dhāraṇī one hundred and eight times over food, medicine, or clean water, and partake of it. All sicknesses and pains will be dissolved immediately."

THE TWELVE GREAT YAKṢA GENERALS

At that moment, among the great assembly, twelve great Yakṣa Generals arose from their seats, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha. They were:

General Kumbhīra  •  General Vajra  •  General Mihira
General Āṇḍīra  •  General Majira  •  General Śāṇḍilya
General Indra  •  General Pajra  •  General Mahoraga
General Sindura  •  General Catura  •  General Vikāra

Each general was accompanied by seven thousand yakṣa subordinates. With one voice, they addressed the Buddha: "World-Honored One! Having heard the name of Medicine Master Vaidūrya Light Tathāgata through Your spiritual power, we no longer fear the lower realms. Together, with single-minded devotion, we take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. We vow to protect all living beings who recite and uphold this sūtra or revere the name of Medicine Master Buddha. We will shield them from all calamities, illnesses, and distress, fulfilling all their righteous aspirations."

The World-Honored One praised the Twelve Yakṣa Generals: "Excellent, excellent, great yakṣa leaders! As you resolve to repay the kindness of Medicine Master Tathāgata, you bestow boundless peace and benefit upon all sentient beings."

When the Buddha concluded this teaching, the great Bodhisattvas, the Śrāvakas, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the entire assembly rejoiced exceedingly, accepted the teaching in faith, bowed reverently, and carried it into practice.

THE THREE REFUGES

I take refuge in the Buddha, wishing that all sentient beings understand the Great Way profoundly and bring forth the supreme Bodhi Mind.
I take refuge in the Dharma, wishing that all sentient beings penetrate the Treasury of Sūtras and attain wisdom as vast as the ocean.
I take refuge in the Sangha, wishing that all sentient beings lead the great assembly in harmony, without any obstruction.

DEDICATION OF MERIT

May the merit and virtue accrued from reciting the Medicine Master Sūtra
Adorn the Buddha’s Pure Lands,
Repaying fourfold kindness above,
And relieving suffering in the three paths below.
May all who see or hear of this
Bring forth the Bodhi Mind,
And when this retribution body is finished,
Be born together in the Land of Pure Peace and Serenity.

tt_kinh_vo_luong_tho.tieu_de: THE SŪTRA ON THE BUDDHA OF IMMEASURABLE LIFE (SUKHĀVATĪVYŪHA)
tt_kinh_vo_luong_tho.tom_tat: The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra, translated from Saṅghavarman's Chinese (BDK English Tripiṭaka Series / Hisao Inagaki), detailing the 48 Great Vows of Dharmākara, the splendors of Sukhāvatī, the 3 Grades of Rebirth, and the instruction to Maitreya on the Five Evils.
tt_kinh_vo_luong_tho.noi_dung:
THE SŪTRA ON THE BUDDHA OF IMMEASURABLE LIFE

(The Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra — Kinh Vô Lượng Thọ Phật)

Translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by Tripiṭaka Master Saṅghavarman of Cao Wei
English Translation referencing the BDK English Tripiṭaka Series (Numata Center / Hisao Inagaki & Harold Stewart)

INCENSE OFFERING & PRAISE

Incense burning in the golden censer,
Fragrant clouds pervade the universe.
The assembly of Buddhas gather like vast oceans,
Bestowing their compassionate presence upon all worlds.
Namo Incense Cloud Canopy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (3 times)

OPENING GĀTHĀ

The supreme, profound, and wondrous Dharma,
In hundreds of thousands of myriad kalpas is rarely encountered.
I now have seen and heard, and am able to receive and uphold it,
May I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.

PART ONE: THE ASSEMBLY ON VULTURE PEAK AND DHARMĀKARA’S VOWS

Thus have I heard. Once the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were renowned Arhats, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Aśvajit, Mahānāma, Yaśodeva, Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, and Ānanda. There were also limitless Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas led by Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and Maitreya, all established in the Mahāyāna, perfected in transcendent virtues and boundless compassion.

At that time, the physical appearance of the World-Honored One was radiantly serene, dignified, and luminous like molten gold, shining with sublime brilliance never seen before. Venerable Ānanda arose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and said: "World-Honored One! Today Your faculties are radiant, joyous, and luminous. You appear like a golden mirror reflecting celestial beauty. Has the World-Honored One entered the meditation of all Buddhas? Does the Tathāgata contemplate past, present, and future Buddhas? Why is Your countenance so exceedingly magnificent?"

The Buddha praised Ānanda, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! Your question springs from deep wisdom and boundless compassion for all living beings. The Tathāgata, with unconditioned great kindness, appears in the world out of pity for beings in the three realms, desiring to rescue them and shower them with true benefit. Listen attentively, Ānanda; I shall now proclaim it to you."

The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the distant past, limitless, measureless eons ago, fifty-three successive Buddhas appeared in the world, beginning with Dīpaṅkara Buddha. The fifty-fourth Buddha was named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata. During his reign, there was a great king who, upon hearing the Dharma, renounced his royal throne, entered the monastic life, and took the Dharma name Dharmākara. Bhikṣu Dharmākara was endowed with transcendent wisdom, courage, and boundless compassion."

"Dharmākara went before Lokeśvararāja Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and praised the Buddha in verse. Then he made this vow: 'World-Honored One, I resolve to attain Unsurpassed Complete Enlightenment. May You expound for me the Dharmas of the pure lands of all Buddhas, so that I may cultivate and establish a supreme, incomparable Buddha-land that surpasses all others.' Lokeśvararāja Buddha then revealed to him the nature, splendor, and adornments of two hundred and ten koṭis of Buddha-lands. Dharmākara concentrated his mind for five full kalpas, selecting the purest and most sublime features of all lands to form forty-eight supreme vows."

THE FORTY-EIGHT GREAT VOWS (HIGHLIGHTS)

1. The Vow of No Evil Destinies: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be in my land hells, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

2. The Vow of No Falling into Evil Destinies: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, humans and devas in my land should fall back into the three evil paths after death, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

3. The Vow of Golden Bodies: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, humans and devas in my land should not all be the color of genuine gold, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

11. The Vow of Abiding in the Right Settled State: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, humans and devas in my land should not dwell in the Definitely Assured State and unerringly reach Nirvāṇa, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

12. The Vow of Boundless Light (Amitābha): 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, my radiant light should be limited, unable to illuminate at least a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

13. The Vow of Boundless Life (Amitāyus): 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, my lifespan should be limited, lasting only a hundred thousand kotis of nayutas of kalpas, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

18. The Primal Vow of Ten Recitations (The Fundamental Vow):
'If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the lands of the ten directions who sincerely and joyfully entrust themselves, aspire to be born in my land, and recite my name even ten times, should not be born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment—excepted only are those who commit the five gravest offenses and slander the True Dharma.'

19. The Vow of Welcoming at Death: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings in the ten directions who bring forth the Bodhi Mind, cultivate wholesome deeds, and sincerely wish to be born in my land, should not at the moment of death see me appear before them surrounded by a great assembly, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

20. The Vow of Rebirth through Mindful Dedication: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, sentient beings who hear my name, direct their thoughts to my land, plant wholesome roots, and sincerely dedicate their merits toward rebirth should not achieve rebirth, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.'

22. The Vow of Reaching Enlightenment in One Lifetime: 'If, when I attain Buddhahood, Bodhisattvas in my land should not eventually reach the stage of Becoming a Buddha in the Next Lifetime (Ekapratibaddhapudgala), may I not attain perfect enlightenment—excepting those who, by their own original vows, wish to manifest in other worlds to deliver sentient beings.'

PART TWO: THE LAND OF ULTIMATE BLISS (SUKHĀVATĪ)

Ānanda asked the Buddha: "Has Dharmākara Bodhisattva already attained Buddhahood, or is he yet to attain it?"

The Buddha replied: "Dharmākara Bodhisattva has already attained Buddhahood and is now dwelling in the Western direction, past a hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-lands, in the realm named Sukhāvatī (Ultimate Bliss). Ten kalpas have passed since his enlightenment. He is known as Amitābha (Boundless Light) and Amitāyus (Boundless Life). His radiance illuminates all Buddha-lands without obstruction, and his lifespan, as well as the lifespan of all beings born in that land, is immeasurable and inexhaustible."

"In that land, the earth is composed entirely of seven jewels: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, amber, and agate. It is flat, soft, fragrant, and vast beyond measure. There are jeweled lotus ponds filled with the water of eight virtues. Jeweled trees line the paths, adorned with pearls and nets of gold bells that produce sublime Dharma melodies when stirred by gentle breezes. Birds of multicolored plumage sing verses on the Five Roots, the Seven Factors of Enlightenment, and the Noble Eightfold Path. Living beings born there never suffer physical sickness, old age, or emotional grief, but progress irreversibly toward Unsurpassed Bodhi."

THE THREE GRADES OF REBIRTH

The Buddha told Ānanda: "Living beings who attain rebirth in that land are divided into three grades:"

The Superior Grade: "Those who leave household life, abandon worldly desires to become monks, bring forth the Bodhi Mind, cultivate pure conduct, and single-mindedly recite Amitābha Buddha's name. At the time of death, Amitābha Buddha, together with the sacred assembly, will manifest directly before them and escort them upon a diamond dais to instantaneous rebirth in the Pure Land."

The Middle Grade: "Those who, although unable to become monks, bring forth the Bodhi Mind, observe the precepts, build stūpas, make offerings to the Triple Gem, practice filial piety, and single-mindedly recite the Buddha’s name with dedication. At death, Amitābha Buddha’s transformation body will manifest and welcome them into the Pure Land."

The Lower Grade: "Those who cannot perform great merits, yet bring forth the Bodhi Mind, joyfully rejoice in the Buddha’s virtues, and single-mindedly recite Amitābha Buddha’s name even ten times. At death, they will see the Buddha in a dream and likewise attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī."

EXHORTATION TO MAITREYA AND THE FIVE EVILS

The Buddha then instructed Maitreya Bodhisattva: "In this Sahā world, sentient beings are tormented by the Five Evils, the Five Sufferings, and the Five Burnings: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxication. They compete for transient wealth, injure one another, and harvest bitter fruits across endless kalpas. Maitreya, you should teach living beings to discipline their bodies, rectify their minds, avoid evil, practice good, and diligently recite Amitābha Buddha’s name to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, escaping the cycle of samsāra forever."

When the World-Honored One expounded this teaching, twelve thousand kotis of nayutas of beings attained the Pure Eye of Dharma, and twenty-two kotis of devas and humans brought forth the Supreme Bodhi Mind. The entire assembly, devas, humans, asuras, and dragon spirits rejoiced with boundless faith and reverently put the teaching into practice.

THE THREE REFUGES

I take refuge in the Buddha, wishing that all sentient beings understand the Great Way profoundly and bring forth the supreme Bodhi Mind.
I take refuge in the Dharma, wishing that all sentient beings penetrate the Treasury of Sūtras and attain wisdom as vast as the ocean.
I take refuge in the Sangha, wishing that all sentient beings lead the great assembly in harmony, without any obstruction.

DEDICATION OF MERIT

May the merit and virtue accrued from reciting the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life
Adorn the Buddha’s Pure Lands,
Repaying fourfold kindness above,
And relieving suffering in the three paths below.
May all who see or hear of this
Bring forth the Bodhi Mind,
And when this retribution body is finished,
Be born together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

tt_kinh_dai_bi_tam_da_la_ni.tom_tat: The Sūtra of the Vast, Perfect, Unimpeded Great Compassion Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, translated by Bhagavaddharma (BTTS / DRBU), containing the 10 Vows, Sanskrit Dharani, 15 Auspicious Rebirths, and the 10 Minds of Bodhi.
tt_kinh_dai_bi_tam_da_la_ni.noi_dung:
THE SŪTRA OF THE DHĀRAṄĪ OF THE GREAT COMPASSIONATE MIND

(Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī Sūtra / Mahākaruṇācitta Dhāraṇī Sūtra — Kinh Đại Bi Tâm Đà La Ni)

Translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by Tripiṭaka Master Bhagavaddharma of the Tang Dynasty
English Translation referencing the Buddhist Text Translation Society (BTTS / Dharma Realm Buddhist University)

INCENSE OFFERING & PRAISE

Incense smoke wafts in curls across the Dharma Realm,
The assembly of Buddhas gather like clouds from afar.
Wherever sincere devotion arises,
The Buddhas manifest their auspicious golden light.
Namo Incense Cloud Canopy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (3 times)

OPENING GĀTHĀ

The supreme, profound, and wondrous Dharma,
In hundreds of thousands of myriad kalpas is rarely encountered.
I now have seen and heard, and am able to receive and uphold it,
May I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.

THE SŪTRA TEXT

Thus have I heard. Once the Buddha Śākyamuni was staying in the jewel-adorned bodhimaṇḍa of the palace of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva on Mount Potalaka. The Buddha sat upon a lion throne adorned with immeasurable jewels, lapis lazuli, and maṇi gems, hung all around with hundreds of banners, pennants, and jeweled canopies.

At that time, the Tathāgata was upon the Dharma seat, preparing to expound the teaching of the vast, perfect, unimpeded Great Compassion Dhāraṇī. Limitless Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas gathered in the assembly, led by Dhāraṇī King Bodhisattva, Jewel King Bodhisattva, Medicine King Bodhisattva, Medicine Superior Bodhisattva, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Flower Adornment Bodhisattva, Great Adornment Bodhisattva, Jewel Treasury Bodhisattva, Virtue Treasury Bodhisattva, Vajra Treasury Bodhisattva, Akāśagarbha Bodhisattva, Maitreya Bodhisattva, and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. All were great Dharma Princes who had received empowerment and abhīṣeka.

There were also limitless great Śrāvakas, arhats including Mahākāśyapa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and Subhūti; as well as the Four Heavenly Kings, Brahmā kings, Śakra, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas. All gathered with utmost reverence.

At that moment, Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara secretly emitted a great supernatural radiance. The golden brilliance illuminated the three-thousand great-thousand world systems, the heavenly palaces, and all the realms of the ten directions. Seeing this wondrous light, Dhāraṇī King Bodhisattva asked the Buddha: "World-Honored One, for what reason does this radiant, magnificent light manifest today?"

The Buddha told Dhāraṇī King Bodhisattva: "Virtuous man, you should know that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva wishes to proclaim the Vast, Perfect, Unimpeded Great Compassion Dhāraṇī to comfort and benefit all living beings. Therefore, he manifests this wondrous sign."

AVALOKITEŚVARA’S RESOLVE AND THE ORIGIN OF THE DHĀRAṆĪ

Then Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva arose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and said: "World-Honored One! I have a mantra of the Great Compassionate Heart and now wish to proclaim it. It is for the purpose of enabling all living beings to obtain peace and joy, to eradicate all illnesses, to prolong life, to gain abundance, to extinguish all heavy sins and offenses, to depart from hindrances and fears, and to swiftly fulfill all pure aspirations."

"World-Honored One! I recall that countless kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world named Thousand-Light Quiet Residence Tathāgata (Sahasraprabhā-śāntiniketa). Out of compassionate regard for me and all living beings, that Buddha transmitted to me this Vast, Perfect, Unimpeded Great Compassion Dhāraṇī. Stroking my crown with his golden hand, he told me: 'Virtuous man, you should uphold this heart-mantra and broadly benefit all living beings in future evil ages.' At that time, I was merely on the First Stage (Pramuditā-bhūmi) of Bodhisattvahood. Upon hearing this dhāraṇī once, I instantly leaped from the First Stage directly to the Eighth Stage (Acalā-bhūmi) of Immovability. Overjoyed, I brought forth this great vow: 'If I can truly benefit and bring peace to all living beings in future ages, may a thousand hands and a thousand eyes immediately manifest upon my body!' As soon as I made this vow, a thousand hands and a thousand eyes instantly appeared upon my person, and the great earth shook in six ways."

THE TEN VOWS OF AVALOKITEŚVARA BODHISATTVA

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said: "If living beings wish to recite and uphold this dhāraṇī, they should first bring forth a compassionate mind for all sentient beings and follow me in making these solemn vows:"

Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I swiftly learn all Dharmas.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I soon obtain the Eye of Wisdom.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I swiftly ferry all beings across to liberation.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I soon obtain skillful means.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I swiftly board the Prajñā Boat.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I soon cross over the ocean of suffering.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I swiftly attain the Path of Precepts and Samādhi.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I soon ascend the Mountain of Nirvāṇa.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I swiftly dwell in the Non-Action Realm.
Namo Great Compassion Avalokiteśvara, may I soon unite with the Dharmakāya Body.

If I go toward a mountain of knives, the knife mountain shatters itself.
If I go toward a boiling cauldron, the boiling cauldron extinguishes itself.
If I go toward the hells, the hells instantly dissipate.
If I go toward hungry ghosts, the hungry ghosts are satisfied.
If I go toward asuras, their hatred transforms into peace.
If I go toward animals, they swiftly attain great wisdom.

THE GREAT COMPASSION DHĀRAṆĪ

(Nīlakaṇṭha Dhāraṇī)

namo ratnatrayāya • namo 'ryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya mahāsattvāya mahākāruṇikāya • oṃ sarva-rabhaye sidhyantu mantra-padāni svāhā • namas-kṛtvā imaṃ aryāvalokiteśvara-stavaṃ nīlakaṇṭha-nāma • hṛdayaṃ vartayiṣyāmi sarvārtha-sādhanaṃ śubham • aje yaṃ sarva-bhūtānāṃ bhava-mārga-viśodhakam • tadyathā: oṃ āloka-lokātīta krānta he hare mahābodhisattva • smara smara hṛdayam • kuru kuru karma • dhara dhara dharani-rāja • cala cala malla-vikrānte • ehy-ehi loka-jiteśvara rāga-viṣa-vināśana • dveṣa-viṣa-vināśana • moha-viṣa-vināśana • hulu hulu mālā • sara sara siri siri suru suru • buddhya buddhya bodhaya bodhaya • maitreya nīlakaṇṭha kāmasya darśanaṃ prahlādaya manaḥ svāhā • siddhāya svāhā • mahāsiddhāya svāhā • siddhayogeśvarāya svāhā • nīlakaṇṭhāya svāhā • varāhamukha-siṃhamukhāya svāhā • padma-hastāya svāhā • cakra-yudhāya svāhā • śaṅkha-śabda-nibodhanāya svāhā • mahā-lakuṭa-dharāya svāhā • vāma-skandha-deśa-sthita-kṛṣṇājināya svāhā • vyāghra-carma-nivasānāya svāhā • namo ratnatrayāya • namo 'ryāvalokiteśvarāya svāhā • oṃ sidhyantu mantra-padāni svāhā.

THE FIFTEEN AUSPICIOUS REBIRTHS AND FREEDOM FROM UNTIMELY DEATH

Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One! If living beings recite and uphold this Great Compassion Dhāraṇī, they will not suffer any of the fifteen kinds of bad deaths, and they will surely obtain the fifteen kinds of auspicious rebirths."

The fifteen bad deaths averted are:
1. They will not die of starvation or deprivation.
2. They will not die from shackles, imprisonment, or caning.
3. They will not die at the hands of enemies or adversaries.
4. They will not die in warfare or battle.
5. They will not die from tigers, wolves, or fierce beasts.
6. They will not die from poisonous snakes, vipers, or scorpions.
7. They will not die from drowning in water or burning in fire.
8. They will not die from toxic poisons or lethal potions.
9. They will not die from sorcery, curses, or black magic.
10. They will not die from madness, madness-inducing illness, or delusion.
11. They will not die from falling from trees or cliffs.
12. They will not die from evil spirits or ghosts draining their vitality.
13. They will not die from pestilence or virulent plagues.
14. They will not die by suicide.
15. They will not die an unnatural or unprepared death.

The fifteen auspicious rebirths obtained are:
1. In every rebirth, they will always meet virtuous rulers and leaders.
2. In every rebirth, they will always be born in peaceful and noble lands.
3. In every rebirth, they will always encounter good seasons and abundance.
4. In every rebirth, they will always meet good spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
5. In every rebirth, their physical faculties will be sound and complete.
6. In every rebirth, their spiritual aspiration (the Bodhi Mind) will be mature and steady.
7. In every rebirth, they will never break the moral precepts.
8. In every rebirth, their relatives and households will live in concord.
9. In every rebirth, their wealth and sustenance will always be sufficient.
10. In every rebirth, they will always receive the respect and reverence of others.
11. In every rebirth, their belongings will never be plundered or stolen.
12. In every rebirth, whatever righteous wishes they seek will all be fulfilled.
13. In every rebirth, devas, nāgas, and protective deities will constantly protect them.
14. In every rebirth, they will hear the Buddha Dharma in the place where they are born.
15. In every rebirth, they will awaken to the profound meaning of the True Dharma and swiftly attain enlightenment.

THE TEN MARKS OF THE DHĀRAṆĪ

Then Dhāraṇī King Bodhisattva asked Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva: "Virtuous one, what are the forms and characteristics of this Great Compassion Dhāraṇī?"

Avalokiteśvara replied: "It is the Mind of Great Compassion, the Mind of Equality, the Mind of Non-Action, the Mind of Non-Attachment, the Mind of Contemplating Emptiness, the Mind of Respect and Reverence, the Mind of Humility, the Mind of Non-Distraction, the Mind of Non-Deliberation, and the Unexcelled Bodhi Mind. Know that these ten minds are the true essence of this Dhāraṇī. One who cultivates in accordance with these minds will surely attain supreme awakening."

When the Buddha expounded this sūtra, the vast assembly, devas, nāgas, humans, and nonhumans rejoiced exceedingly, bowed to the Buddha, and resolved to uphold the teaching forever.

THE THREE REFUGES

I take refuge in the Buddha, wishing that all sentient beings understand the Great Way profoundly and bring forth the supreme Bodhi Mind.
I take refuge in the Dharma, wishing that all sentient beings penetrate the Treasury of Sūtras and attain wisdom as vast as the ocean.
I take refuge in the Sangha, wishing that all sentient beings lead the great assembly in harmony, without any obstruction.

DEDICATION OF MERIT

May the merit and virtue accrued from reciting the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī Sūtra
Adorn the Buddha’s Pure Lands,
Repaying fourfold kindness above,
And relieving suffering in the three paths below.
May all who see or hear of this
Bring forth the Bodhi Mind,
And when this retribution body is finished,
Be born together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

tt_nghi_quy_tuy_cau_tuc_dac.noi_dung:
THE RITUAL MANUAL OF THE MAHĀPRATISARĀ DHĀRAṄĪ

(Vajraśekhara-Yoga: The Supreme Secret Attainment of Buddhahood through the Wish-Fulfilling Dhāraṇī — Taishō No. 1153)

Translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra (Bukong) of the Tang Dynasty
English Translation referencing the BDK English Tripiṭaka Series & Academic Sanskrit Editions

INCENSE OFFERING & PRAISE

The pure jewel-incense is ignited,
Fragrant clouds spread throughout the Vajradhātu realm.
May all obstacles and misfortunes be dissolved,
And all wholesome wishes be instantaneously fulfilled.
Namo Incense Cloud Canopy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (3 times)

THE RITUAL PROCEDURE & EXHORTATION

At that time, in the great assembly of Vairocana Buddha, the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Evil Destinies (Sarvadurgatipariśodhana) arose from his seat, joined his palms reverently, and addressed the Bhagavān: "World-Honored One! In future evil ages of the Five Turbidities, living beings will commit numerous unwholesome deeds, fall into serious offenses, and suffer terrible retributions. By what skillful means can they swiftly extinguish grave karmic obstacles, fulfill their vows, and attain the supreme fruit of Buddhahood?"

Vairocana Buddha smiled and radiated boundless light from his crown, proclaiming: "Listen well, Bodhisattva! There is a supreme esoteric dhāraṇī named Mahāpratisarā (The Great Wish-Fulfilling Dhāraṇī). It is the heart-essence of all Tathāgatas. If one writes this dhāraṇī upon fine birch bark or silk and wears it on the body or neck, or recites it with single-minded sincerity, all five deadly sins and gravest offenses will be dissolved like frost in the morning sun. No weapons, poisons, wild beasts, curses, or demonic spirits will ever be able to harm that person. Whatever wholesome desires they seek—whether wealth, health, offspring, wisdom, or liberation—will be granted without exception."

THE MAHĀPRATISARĀ FUNDAMENTAL DHĀRAṆĪ (SANSKRIT ESSENCE)

oṃ maṇi-vajre hṛdaya-vajre māra-sainyavidrāvani hana hana sarva-śatrūn dahana dahana sarva-pāpān matha matha sarva-duṣṭān hūm hūm phaṭ phaṭ svāhā • oṃ vimale jaya-vare amṛte hūm hūm phaṭ phaṭ svāhā • oṃ bhara bhara saṃbhara saṃbhara indriya-viśodhani hūm hūm ruru cale svāhā • oṃ sarva-tathāgatābhiṣeka-samaya-śriye hūm hūm phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.

THE SEVENFOLD BENEFITS & PROTECTION

The Buddha expounded the marvelous qualities of the Mahāpratisarā Dhāraṇī:

1. Liberation from Lower Realms: Even if a being has fallen into the Avīci Hell, if someone casts the sand empowered by this mantra upon their tomb or body, they will immediately ascend to the heavenly realms.

2. Invulnerability to Curses and Sorcery: All black magic, demonic incantations, and venomous poisons become neutralized and transform into medicine.

3. Safety in Perils: Travelers carrying this mantra are safeguarded against shipwrecks, bandits, fire, floods, and military combat.

4. Fulfillment of Pure Prayers: Barren women obtain virtuous children; the impoverished gain abundance; the sick recover vigor.

THE THREE REFUGES & DEDICATION

I take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
May the merit of upholding the Mahāpratisarā Dhāraṇī
Disperse all fears and karmic debts,
May all living beings be peaceful and swiftly attain Buddhahood.

tt_kinh_nhap_nhu_lai_tri_duc_bat_tu_nghi.tieu_de: MAHĀVAIPULYA SŪTRA ON ENTERING THE INCONCEIVABLE WISDOM OF THE TATHĀGATA
tt_kinh_nhap_nhu_lai_tri_duc_bat_tu_nghi.tom_tat: The Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāra Sūtra (Śikṣānanda / BDK), detailing how Bodhisattvas enter the inconceivable realm of non-dual wisdom and universal liberation.
tt_kinh_nhap_nhu_lai_tri_duc_bat_tu_nghi.noi_dung:
THE MAHĀVAIPULYA SŪTRA ON ENTERING THE INCONCEIVABLE REALM OF THE TATHĀGATA'S WISDOM AND VIRTUES

(Tathāgataguṇajñānācintyaviṣayāvatāra Sūtra — Taishō Tripiṭaka No. 301)

Translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of the Tang Dynasty
English Translation referencing the BDK English Tripiṭaka Series & Kalavinka Buddhist Classics

INCENSE OFFERING & OPENING GĀTHĀ

The supreme, profound, and wondrous Dharma,
In hundreds of thousands of myriad kalpas is rarely encountered.
I now have seen and heard, and am able to receive and uphold it,
May I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.

THE SŪTRA TEXT

Thus have I heard. Once the Buddha was staying in the Hall of Universal Luminous Radiance (Prabhāsaprabhā) in the Bodhimaṇḍa of Quiescence in the country of Magadha. This was the exalted place where all Buddhas realize supreme enlightenment. Surrounding the Bhagavān were limitless Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, arhats, devas, nāgas, and spiritual kings, all adorned with pure merits and wisdom.

At that time, from the uṣṇīṣa of the Tathāgata, a great ray of light shone forth named Universal Illumination of Inconceivable Wisdom. It illuminated all Buddha-lands across the ten directions. In that light, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva arose, knelt before the Buddha, and requested the World-Honored One to expound how a Bodhisattva enters the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata's wisdom and virtues.

The Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Virtuous man! The wisdom and virtues of the Tathāgata are neither produced nor destroyed; they do not come and do not go. Like space, they pervade all dharmas, yet remain unstained by any characteristics. A Bodhisattva who contemplates that all phenomena are empty, signless, and unconditioned enters directly into the ocean of the Tathāgata's wisdom. In that state, there is no duality between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, no distinction between self and others. With such wisdom, one manifests boundless transformation bodies throughout the worlds of the ten directions to deliver all suffering beings without ever leaving the stillness of the Dharmakāya."

When this profound teaching was proclaimed, limitless Bodhisattvas attained the Samādhi of Entering the Inconceivable Realm, and countless beings brought forth the unexcelled Bodhi Mind. The assembly bowed reverently and rejoiced with boundless devotion.

THE THREE REFUGES & DEDICATION

I take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
May the merit of this profound teaching illuminate all minds,
Awakening all living beings to their inherent Buddha Nature.

tt_kinh_tuy_cau_tuc_dac_dai_tu_tai.tieu_de: SŪTRA OF THE MAHĀPRATISARĀ GREAT SOVEREIGN DHĀRAṄĪ
tt_kinh_tuy_cau_tuc_dac_dai_tu_tai.tom_tat: The Mahāpratisarā Dhāraṇī Sūtra (Ratnacinta / BDK), proclaimed on Vulture Peak to Mahābrahmā on the supreme protective powers and wish-fulfilling virtues of the dhāraṇī.
tt_kinh_tuy_cau_tuc_dac_dai_tu_tai.noi_dung:
THE SŪTRA OF THE MAHĀPRATISARĀ GREAT SOVEREIGN WISH-FULFILLING DHĀRAṆĪ

(Taishō Tripiṭaka No. 1154)

Translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by Master Ratnacinta (Bao Siwei) of the Tang Dynasty
English Translation referencing the BDK English Tripiṭaka Series & Academic Sanskrit Sources

INCENSE OFFERING & PRAISE

Sandalwood incense purifies the shrine,
Fragrant clouds reach the myriad worlds.
The Buddhas bestow supreme blessings and peace upon all.
Namo Incense Cloud Canopy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (3 times)

THE SŪTRA TEXT

Thus have I heard. Once the Bhagavān was staying on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa near Rājagṛha, expounding the Dharma for an assembly of limitless disciples, Bodhisattvas, and celestial kings. At that time, Mahābrahmā, Sovereign of the Sahā World, accompanied by countless heavenly beings, arrived before the Buddha, circumambulated him three times, knelt with joined palms, and said:

"World-Honored One! Living beings in this world are constantly afflicted by diseases, poverty, demonic harassment, and unexpected disasters. We pray that the World-Honored One will proclaim the Great Sovereign Dhāraṇī of Mahāpratisarā, which grants protection and fulfills all desires, so that living beings may dwell in lasting safety."

The Buddha told Mahābrahmā: "Listen with utmost care, Brahmā! This Mahāpratisarā Great Sovereign Dhāraṇī possesses invincible spiritual power. It is proclaimed by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time. If a person upholds, recites, or wears this mantra, all heavenly kings, Four Guardian Kings, and vajra guardians will shield them day and night. Their offenses of countless kalpas will vanish immediately, and whatever wholesome wishes they cherish will be granted in full."

oṃ maṇi-dhāri vajriṇi mahā-pratisare hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.

When the Buddha concluded this proclamation, Mahābrahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the assembly of devas and humans rejoiced, bowed to the Buddha, and resolved to protect this sūtra throughout the universe.

DEDICATION OF MERIT

May the merit accrued from this recitation
Eradicate all misfortunes and grant peace to all living beings.
May all beings leave suffering behind and attain supreme enlightenment.

tt_kinh_cuu_bat_nga_quy_diem_khau.tieu_de: SŪTRA ON THE DHĀRAṄĪ FOR RESCUING FLAMING-MOUTH HUNGRY GHOSTS (ULKĀMUKHA)
tt_kinh_cuu_bat_nga_quy_diem_khau.tom_tat: The Ulkāmukha Dhāraṇī Sūtra, translated by Amoghavajra (BDK English Tripiṭaka Series / Charles D. Orzech), detailing the origin of the Food Bestowal liturgy, the rescue of Ānanda, the Food-Multiplying Dhāraṇī, and the names of the Four Tathāgatas.
tt_kinh_cuu_bat_nga_quy_diem_khau.noi_dung:
THE SŪTRA PROCLAIMED BY THE BUDDHA ON THE DHĀRAṆĪ FOR RESCUING THE FLAMING-MOUTH HUNGRY GHOSTS

(Ulkāmukha Dhāraṇī Sūtra — Taishō Tripiṭaka No. 1313)

Translated from Sanskrit into Chinese by Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra (Bukong) of the Tang Dynasty
English Translation referencing the BDK English Tripiṭaka Series (Numata Center / Charles D. Orzech)

INCENSE OFFERING & PRAISE

Incense burning in the golden censer,
Fragrant clouds pervade the ten directions.
May all suffering beings in the lower paths
Receive the soothing nectar of the Dharma and attain release.
Namo Incense Cloud Canopy Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. (3 times)

OPENING GĀTHĀ

The supreme, profound, and wondrous Dharma,
In hundreds of thousands of myriad kalpas is rarely encountered.
I now have seen and heard, and am able to receive and uphold it,
May I understand the Tathāgata’s true meaning.

THE SŪTRA TEXT

Thus have I heard. Once the World-Honored One was staying at the Nyagrodha Monastery near Kapilavastu, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus, Bodhisattvas, devas, nāgas, and humans who respectfully circled the Buddha to listen to his Dharma teaching.

At that time, Venerable Ānanda was sitting quietly in solitary meditation in a secluded place. During the third watch of the night, Ānanda suddenly saw a hungry ghost (preta) named Ulkāmukha (Flaming Mouth) standing before him. The creature was terrifying in appearance: his body was withered and blackened, his throat was as narrow as a needle, blazing fire constantly surged from his mouth, his hair was disheveled, and his limbs were like dry twigs.

The hungry ghost addressed Ānanda, saying: "Venerable Ānanda! Three days from now, your lifespan in this world will be exhausted. Upon death, you will surely be reborn among us in the realm of hungry ghosts, bearing a body like mine and suffering endless torment!"

Hearing these words, Ānanda was gripped by intense terror and distress. His hair stood on end, and he asked: "Ghost! By what skillful means or merit may I escape this dreadful destiny?"

Ulkāmukha replied: "Tomorrow morning, if you can bestow food upon hundreds of thousands of nayutas of hungry ghosts, and offer food and drink to hundreds of thousands of brahmans and ascetics, dedicating the merit to the Triple Gem, your lifespan will be extended, your blessings will increase, and I too shall escape the agonizing suffering of the ghost realm and be reborn in heaven."

Overcome with sorrow and fear, Ānanda rose swiftly and hurried to the World-Honored One. He bowed deeply at the Buddha's feet, trembling, and recounted the preta's warning, saying: "World-Honored One! How can I, a solitary monk, provide sufficient food and drink for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of hungry ghosts and sages? We pray that the World-Honored One will compassionately bestow a method of salvation!"

THE TRANSMISSION OF THE FOOD-BESTOWING DHĀRAṆĪ

The Buddha comforted Ānanda, saying: "Fear not, Ānanda! In the past, when I was practicing the Bodhisattva Way, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva transmitted to me a supreme dhāraṇī named The Immeasurable Majestic Virtue, Freedom and Ease, Bright King of Tathāgatas (Apramāṇaguṇa-sarvalokajiteśvara Dhāraṇī). Through the spiritual power of this mantra, even a single mouthful or small bowl of pure food and clean water, when consecrated, multiplies into limitless ocean-like vessels of sweet dew (amṛta) and celestial delicacies, sufficient to thoroughly satisfy hundreds of thousands of kotis of hungry ghosts in the ten directions, eradicating their fire of hunger and thirst, and guiding them to rebirth in heavenly realms or the Pure Land."

"Ānanda, if any bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā wishes to prolong life, increase wisdom, remove karmic obstacles, and rescue ancestors and unseen spirits, they should place a small portion of clean water and food in a clean vessel, recite this dhāraṇī seven times, snap their fingers, and scatter the food upon clean ground. Immediately, all hungry ghosts throughout the ten directions will partake of this supreme feast."

namo sarva tathāgatāvalokite oṃ saṃbhāra saṃbhāra hūṃ.

THE HOLY NAMES OF THE FOUR TATHĀGATAS

The Buddha told Ānanda: "When bestowing food, one should also recite the names of the Four Tathāgatas, which bestow profound empowerment:"

1. Namo Many Treasures Tathāgata (Prabhūtaratna): Hearing His name, all hungry ghosts are freed from karmic poverty and obtain abundant treasures of blessings and wisdom.

2. Namo Exquisite Form Tathāgata (Surūpakāya): Hearing His name, all ghosts shed their ugly, deformed, and withered forms, attaining radiant, handsome celestial bodies.

3. Namo Vast Body Tathāgata (Vipulakāya): Hearing His name, their constricted throats open wide, their bellies shrink to normal proportions, and they partake of sweet ambrosia without burning obstruction.

4. Namo Fearless Tathāgata (Abhayaṅkara): Hearing His name, all terrifying fears, enmity, and malice cease immediately, and they are never again reborn in the three evil paths.

"Furthermore, when one additionally invokes Namo Sweet Dew King Tathāgata (Amṛtarāja / Amitābha), the cool waters of enlightenment sprinkle upon their heads, dissolving all karmic offenses and guiding them directly to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī)."

When Ānanda and the great assembly heard the Buddha proclaim this profound sūtra, they rejoiced exceedingly, bowed with reverence, and vowed to uphold and practice it faithfully.

THE THREE REFUGES

I take refuge in the Buddha, wishing that all sentient beings understand the Great Way profoundly and bring forth the supreme Bodhi Mind.
I take refuge in the Dharma, wishing that all sentient beings penetrate the Treasury of Sūtras and attain wisdom as vast as the ocean.
I take refuge in the Sangha, wishing that all sentient beings lead the great assembly in harmony, without any obstruction.

DEDICATION OF MERIT

May the merit and virtue of bestowing food upon hungry spirits
Universally benefit all sentient beings in the six realms.
May all departed spirits and karmic creditors
Be liberated from suffering and born together in the Pure Land.

FOREWORD

This Pure Land treatise is, to our knowledge, the first and only compendium of Pure land teaching and thought currently available in a Western language. In the tradition of theAvatamsaka Sutra (which D.T. Suzuki described as the epitome of Buddhist thought, sentiment and experience), the author sometimes shifts from one plane of meaning to another, at times down-to-earth, at times metaphysical, so as to reach readers at every level and to sever attachment to his very words. It is in this light that certain paradoxes already familiar to students of Zen (illusory but not non-existent, recitation with no thought of recitation, etc.) should be viewed and understood.

While the primary focus of this treatise is Pure Land theory and practice, more than half of the book is devoted to questions of concern to all Buddhist schools. Therefore, we suggest the following approach to reading the text, according to the background of the reader:

  • Zen School: Chapters VII to IX first.
  • Tantrism: Chapters VI to X first.
  • Pure Land: Chapters I to V first.
  • The bereaved: Chapter X.
  • All others: Note on Pure Land and Epilogue.

The reader might also familiarize himself with a number of key concepts explained in the Glossary (Amitabha, Awakening vs. Enlightenment, Buddha Recitation, Merit and Virtue, Noumenon/phenomena[1], Pure Land, etc.).

Whatever his approach, he will be forever enriched. Once reborn in the Pure Land, like the proverbial seeker of the Way, he will not only discover the treasure trove (Great Awakening), but also, in time, partake at will of its priceless gems (attain Enlightenment) -- for the common benefit of all sentient beings.

Van Hien Study Group

NOTE ON THE PURE LAND

Of the various forms of Buddhism that developed after the demise of the historical Buddha in 480 B.C., Mahayana (the "Great Vehicle") became the dominant tradition in East and parts of Southeast Asia. This broad area encompasses China, Korea, Vietnam and Japan, among other countries.

In time, a number of schools arose within Mahayana Buddhism in accordance with the capacities and circumstances of the people, the main ones being the Zen, Pure Land and Esoteric schools. Among these schools, Pure land has the greatest number of adherents, although its teachings and methodology are not widely known in the West.

Given its popular appeal, [Pure Land] quickly became the object of the most dominant form of Buddhist devotion in East Asia. (M. Eliade, ed., Encyclopedia of Religions, Vol. 12.)

The present book, part of a series published by the Sutra Translation Committee of the United States and Canada, is a modest attempt to enlarge the understanding of East Asian Buddhism, which (with the possible exception of some segments of Japanese Buddhism) is essentially eclectic in approach and outlook.

What is Pure Land?

[Pure Land comprises the schools] of East Asia which emphasize aspect of Mahayana Buddhism stressing faith in Amida, meditation on and recitation of his name, and the religious goal of being reborn in his "Pure Land," or "Western paradise." (Keith Crim, general editor, Perennial Dictionary of World Religions, p. 586).

In practice, the most common technique of the Pure Land school is the recitation of Amitabha Buddha's name.

Along with this popular form of Pure Land, there is also a higher aspect, in which Amitabha, the Buddha of Infinite Light and Life, is equated with our Buddha Nature, infinitely bright and everlasting (Self-Nature Amitabha, Mind-Only Pure Land).[2]

 

Pure Land: a Compassionate Tradition

Several main elements define Pure Land:

Its teachings are based on compassion, on faith in the compassionate Vows of Amitabha Buddha to welcome and guide all sentient beings who so desire to His Pure Land;

It is an easy method, in terms of both goal (rebirth in the Western Pure Land as a stepping-stone toward Buddhahood) and form of cultivation (can be practiced anywhere, any time with no special liturgy, accoutrements or guidance);

It is a panacea for the diseases of the mind, unlike other methods or meditations which are directed to specific illnesses (for instance, meditation on the corpse is designed to sever lust, while counting the breath is for the purpose of reining in the wandering mind);

It is a democratic method that empowers its adherents, freeing them from arcane metaphysics as well as dependence on teachers, gurus, roshis and other mediating authority figures.[3]

For these reasons, since the thirteenth century, Pure Land has been the dominant tradition in East Asia, playing a crucial role in the democratization of Buddhism and the rise of the lay movement. Honen Shonin (1133-1212), the Patriarch of the Jodo (Pure Land) school in Japan, expressed the very essence of Pure Land teaching when he wrote:

There shall be no distinction, no regard to male or female, good or bad, exalted or lowly; none shall fail to be in his Land of Purity after having called, with complete faith, on Amida.[4] (Quoted by Elizabeth ten Grotenhuis in Joji Okazaki, Pure Land Buddhist Painting, p. 14.)
